question: Why does home assessment differ from a hospital examination?

options.A: Hospital equipment is always brought into the home
options.B: Nurses have less clinical responsibility in home settings
options.C: The home environment directly impacts the patient's daily health
options.D: Patients are always fully recovered during home visits

explanation: Evaluating a patient where they live reveals environmental and social factors that hospitals completely mask. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h1)

question: A major hazard checked during a home safety evaluation is:

options.A: Loose rugs and unlit hallways
options.B: The brand of the television set
options.C: The color of the exterior walls
options.D: The presence of indoor house plants

explanation: Tripping hazards like loose rugs and poor lighting directly increase the risk of falls in vulnerable patients. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h2)

question: What should the nurse check first when entering the patient's bathroom?

options.A: The water pressure of the showerhead
options.B: The expiry date of liquid hand soap
options.C: The decorative color scheme of the tiles
options.D: Presence of grab bars and non-slip mats

explanation: Bathrooms are high-risk zones for slips and falls, making supportive safety installations the priority check. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h2)

question: How should a nurse handle ambient noise during home auscultation?

options.A: Skip listening to heart and lung sounds entirely
options.B: Increase stethoscope pressure to block out room noise
options.C: Minimize household distractions to clearly hear breath sounds
options.D: Rely solely on visual inspection instead of auscultation

explanation: Background noise like radios or talking makes hearing subtle respiratory or cardiac sounds difficult, requiring a quiet environment. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which physical assessment technique involves feeling body tissues with the hands?

options.A: Palpation
options.B: Percussion
options.C: Inspection
options.D: Auscultation

explanation: Palpation uses touch to evaluate texture, temperature, moisture, and swelling of body tissues. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which task is classified as an Activity of Daily Living (ADL)?

options.A: Feeding oneself
options.B: Managing finances
options.C: Shopping for groceries
options.D: Cooking meals

explanation: Feeding, bathing, and dressing are fundamental self-care tasks categorized as basic Activities of Daily Living. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why are Instrumental Activities of Daily Living assessed in home care?

options.A: They test the patient's ability to hear high-pitched sounds
options.B: They calculate the precise caloric intake of the client
options.C: They measure exact muscle strength in the lower limbs
options.D: They determine if the patient can safely manage independent living

explanation: IADLs involve more complex cognitive and physical skills required to live independently in the community. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the first step of a proper home medication review?

options.A: Throwing away all medications older than one month
options.B: Gathering all current bottles, supplements, and OTC drugs
options.C: Writing a brand new prescription chart for the client
options.D: Calling the pharmacy to cancel active prescriptions

explanation: A complete physical check of every medicine the patient actually has at home prevents dangerous drug omissions or overlaps. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why do home care patients frequently experience medication mix-ups?

options.A: Nurses fail to write any instructions on drug bottles
options.B: They often receive prescriptions from multiple different doctors
options.C: Over-the-counter drugs are illegal for home care clients
options.D: Pharmacies always deliver the wrong medication types

explanation: Seeing multiple specialists without centralized tracking often leads to duplicate therapies and conflicting drug schedules. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h5)

question: How can a home care nurse best verify a patient's true dietary access?

options.A: Ask family members about grocery prices in the local market
options.B: Review standard nutritional textbooks used in nursing school
options.C: Inspect the kitchen pantry and refrigerator contents directly
options.D: Assume the client eats three balanced meals daily

explanation: Visual inspection of stored food provides accurate insight into actual nutrition availability compared to patient recall. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h6)

question: Which clinical sign points toward dehydration in an elderly client?

options.A: Dry oral mucous membranes
options.B: Increased daily urine output
options.C: Swelling in both lower legs
options.D: Elevated blood pressure readings

explanation: Dry mouth and mucous membranes are classic indicators of inadequate fluid intake and dehydration. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h6)

question: When should the home care nurse document assessment findings?

options.A: Only when a family member requests notes
options.B: Promptly after completing the home visit
options.C: Before entering the patient's house
options.D: At the end of the work week

explanation: Immediate documentation ensures details remain accurate and clinical changes are communicated without delay. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why are vague charting phrases like 'patient doing fine' discouraged?

options.A: They cause patients to become overly anxious
options.B: They take too long to write in the patient chart
options.C: They fail to provide specific, measurable clinical data
options.D: They are banned by federal health insurance agencies

explanation: Clear documentation requires objective observations so other healthcare team members can track true health status changes. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T6#GNS324_U3_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a home nutritional assessment?

options.A: To test the patient for rare metabolic genetic disorders
options.B: To calculate the exact daily hospital food budget
options.C: To prescribe expensive dietary supplements for the patient
options.D: To evaluate eating habits and home environment factors

explanation: Home assessments look at real-world eating habits, kitchen safety, and environmental factors affecting food intake. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why must a home care nurse check food storage during a nutritional assessment?

options.A: To see if the client can safely store and access food
options.B: To check if the family is hiding food from the nurse
options.C: To ensure the refrigerator meets hospital regulatory standards
options.D: To determine the exact market price of local food items

explanation: Checking food storage reveals whether the client can independently reach, store, and preserve meals safely at home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h1)

question: What percentage of unintentional weight loss over one month is a major red flag?

options.A: Fifteen percent
options.B: Fifty percent
options.C: Twenty-five percent
options.D: Five percent

explanation: Weight loss exceeding five percent of total body weight over a single month indicates a high malnutrition risk. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h2)

question: An overweight elderly client shows muscle wasting in the temples. What does this indicate?

options.A: The client is getting optimal daily protein intake
options.B: The client is experiencing a normal aging process
options.C: The client may still be suffering from malnutrition
options.D: The client has normal fat and muscle distribution

explanation: Overweight individuals can experience protein-energy malnutrition, visible through muscle wasting despite high body fat. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h2)

question: Why should home care nurses incorporate local staples into therapeutic diets?

options.A: To ensure the patient actually follows the dietary plan
options.B: To replace modern medicine with traditional herbal remedies
options.C: To eliminate the need for any professional nutritional advice
options.D: To force the family to spend less money on groceries

explanation: Diets that respect cultural preferences and local food availability are much more likely to be accepted and sustained by the client. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h3)

question: Which adjustment is most appropriate for a client requiring a low-sodium diet?

options.A: Increasing the daily consumption of processed canned foods
options.B: Eliminating all forms of protein from the daily meal plan
options.C: Replacing all drinking water with commercially bottled mineral water
options.D: Using local herbs and natural spices instead of excess bouillon cubes

explanation: Bouillon cubes and commercial seasonings are high in sodium, making natural herbs a healthier flavor alternative. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is the correct seating angle for a client during oral feeding?

options.A: Forty-five degrees semi-fowler
options.B: Ninety degrees upright
options.C: Thirty degrees low-fowler
options.D: Flat on the back

explanation: Sitting upright at a 90-degree angle uses gravity to help direct food safely down the esophagus instead of the trachea. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h4)

question: What sign strongly suggests that a client is struggling with swallowing safety?

options.A: Asking for an extra glass of water with the meal
options.B: A wet-sounding voice quality immediately after swallowing
options.C: Chewing food slowly before attempting to swallow it
options.D: Finishing the entire meal plate within ten minutes

explanation: A wet or gurgling voice after eating indicates that liquid or food residue has pooled near the vocal cords due to unsafe swallowing. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h4)

question: What is the primary reason for flushing an enteral feeding tube with water?

options.A: To prevent tube blockage and provide hydration
options.B: To test the pH balance of digestive stomach acids
options.C: To cool down warm formula before it enters the stomach
options.D: To force trapped air bubbles out of the gastric lining

explanation: Water flushes clear residual formula from the lumen of the tube, stopping clogs and contributing to daily fluid requirements. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why is strict hygiene critical when preparing enteral tube feeds at home?

options.A: Domestic tap water always contains high levels of industrial waste
options.B: Commercial formulas contain toxic chemicals that require washing
options.C: Plastic feeding tubes degrade quickly when exposed to dirty hands
options.D: Liquid formulas support rapid bacterial growth at room temperature

explanation: Nutrient-rich formulas provide an ideal medium for bacteria to multiply quickly, risking severe gastrointestinal infection. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h5)

question: Which complication is most commonly linked to rapid infusion rates of enteral formula?

options.A: Constipation
options.B: Skin rash
options.C: Hypertension
options.D: Diarrhea

explanation: Infusing formula too quickly overwhelms the digestive capacity of the intestines, frequently triggering cramping and diarrhea. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h6)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take if aspiration is suspected during feeding?

options.A: Offer the client a sip of clean water to clear the throat
options.B: Increase the speed of the remaining formula feed
options.C: Stop the feeding immediately and prepare to suction
options.D: Lower the bed flat to help the client relax

explanation: Stopping the feed prevents further material from entering the airway, and suctioning clears the respiratory tract to protect oxygenation. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h6)

question: What is the main benefit of using the return demonstration method for caregiver training?

options.A: It proves the caregiver can safely perform the skill independently
options.B: It eliminates the need for any written nursing care plans
options.C: It reduces the financial cost of purchasing feeding equipment
options.D: It allows the family to diagnose complex clinical diseases

explanation: Watching a caregiver perform a task ensures they understand the steps correctly and can replicate them safely at home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h7)

question: What educational tool is most helpful for caregivers with low literacy levels?

options.A: Complex research journals
options.B: Dense medical textbooks
options.C: Detailed financial spreadsheets
options.D: Simple pictorial guides

explanation: Visual pictures and diagrams help bridge literacy gaps, ensuring instructions remain clear and accessible to all family members. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h7)

question: Which healthcare professional is primarily consulted for specialized dietary adjustments in home care?

options.A: Dietitian
options.B: Physiotherapist
options.C: Laboratory technician
options.D: Pharmacist

explanation: Dietitians specialize in nutritional science and therapeutic meal planning to address specific client deficiencies or medical needs. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h8)

question: A home care nurse notices a steady drop in a client's weight over three visits. What is the best next step?

options.A: Wait until the next scheduled annual medical checkup
options.B: Advise the family to stop all feeding until weight stabilizes
options.C: Discharge the client from home care services immediately
options.D: Document the trend and collaborate with the interdisciplinary team

explanation: Consistent weight loss requires immediate documentation and teamwork to review the care plan and intervene before severe malnutrition develops. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h8)

question: What does the term ambulation primarily refer to in nursing practice?

options.A: Passive range of motion
options.B: Bedside stretching exercises
options.C: The act of walking
options.D: Manual muscle testing

explanation: Ambulation specifically means walking, which is a key milestone in patient recovery and functional independence. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why is early mobility important for patients recovering from an illness?

options.A: It shortens visiting hours for family members
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for pain medication
options.C: It removes the requirement for nursing documentation
options.D: It prevents rapid physical decline caused by bed rest

explanation: Prolonged bed rest triggers negative physical changes across multiple body systems that early movement helps counteract. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which body system provides the rigid framework and leverage points for body movement?

options.A: Skeletal system
options.B: Integumentary system
options.C: Lymphatic system
options.D: Endocrine system

explanation: Bones and joints form the structural skeleton that acts as a system of levers activated by muscle contraction. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary function of proprioception during physical movement?

options.A: Sensing body position in space for balance
options.B: Regulating blood pressure during heavy exertion
options.C: Producing red blood cells inside long bones
options.D: Filtering waste products from contracting muscles

explanation: Proprioceptors in muscles and joints send continuous feedback to the brain regarding body position, ensuring coordinated movement. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of using the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test?

options.A: Measuring maximum oxygen uptake during exercise
options.B: Determining the exact bone density of the hip
options.C: Assessing fine motor skills in the upper extremities
options.D: Evaluating a patient's mobility and fall risk

explanation: The TUG test measures the seconds it takes for a patient to stand up from a chair, walk three meters, turn, and sit back down. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h3)

question: A patient becomes dizzy and short of breath while walking down the hallway. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Administer a prescribed rescue inhaler immediately
options.B: Encourage the patient to walk faster to finish quickly
options.C: Safely assist the patient to a seated position
options.D: Document the symptoms later at the nursing station

question: On which side of the body should a patient hold a single-point cane?

options.A: Behind the back
options.B: The strong side
options.C: Either shoulder
options.D: The weak side

explanation: Holding the cane on the strong side allows the patient to lean weight onto the device while moving the weaker leg. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: Which assistive device is best for a patient who needs a wide base of support due to severe balance issues?

options.A: Cane
options.B: Walker
options.C: Transfer board
options.D: Gait belt

explanation: Walkers surround the patient with a sturdy metal frame, offering much greater stability than a cane. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: Where should a nurse hold a gait belt when helping an unsteady patient walk?

options.A: From underneath the belt using an upward grip
options.B: By looping a finger loosely through the belt buckle
options.C: From the top edge pushing downward on the spine
options.D: From the side while walking two steps ahead

explanation: Grasping the gait belt from underneath provides a secure hold to support the patient's weight if balance is lost. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: What is an important body mechanics rule when helping a patient move from a bed to a chair?

options.A: Bending directly at the waist with straight knees
options.B: Keeping the patient close to your center of gravity
options.C: Keeping your feet close together to increase rotation speed
options.D: Twisting your torso quickly to pivot in one motion

explanation: Keeping the patient close reduces strain on the nurse's lower back and provides better control during the transfer. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: What is a primary nursing action to prevent pressure ulcers in a bedridden patient?

options.A: Repositioning the patient every two hours
options.B: Restricting fluid intake to keep skin dry
options.C: Massaging reddened skin areas vigorously
options.D: Applying dry heat lamps to bony prominences

explanation: Frequent repositioning relieves sustained pressure on blood vessels, preventing tissue damage and breakdown. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: Why does prolonged bed rest increase the risk of deep vein thrombosis (blood clots)?

options.A: Increased production of red blood cells by bone marrow
options.B: Rapid constriction of peripheral arteries from cold air
options.C: Loss of calcium from the skeletal system into the blood
options.D: Stagnation of blood flow in the lower extremities

explanation: Without the pumping action of moving leg muscles, blood flow slows down, creating an environment where clots can easily form. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary focus of disease prevention in home care?

options.A: Eliminating the need for medication in elderly patients

options.C: Reducing hospital building maintenance costs significantly
options.D: Replacing all hospital services with domestic nursing visits

explanation: Home care aims to intercept disease progression through early intervention and lifestyle management within the home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why must clinical protocols be adapted for the home environment?

options.A: Standard hospital equipment is too lightweight for domestic use
options.B: Family members must legally perform all physician duties at home
options.C: Domestic settings often lack the abundant resources found in hospital wards
options.D: Patients prefer ignoring clinical guidelines when inside their own homes

explanation: Nurses must modify their approach because home environments do not have the immediate technology and supply access of a hospital. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h1)

question: Removing loose rugs to prevent falls in an elderly home is an example of what?

options.A: Acute care management
options.B: Secondary prevention
options.C: Primary prevention
options.D: Tertiary prevention

explanation: Primary prevention stops an adverse event or disease from occurring in the first place by modifying the environment or lifestyle. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h2)

question: A home health nurse checks a diabetic patient's feet for early sores. Which level of prevention is this?

options.A: Tertiary prevention
options.B: Primary prevention
options.C: Secondary prevention
options.D: Palliative prevention

explanation: Screening and early detection of existing conditions or complications fall squarely under secondary prevention. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h2)

question: What should a home health assessment include besides physical vital signs?

options.A: Inspection of local commercial transport and taxi availability
options.B: Inventory of neighboring houses and community water supplies
options.C: Review of structural zoning laws for the residential street
options.D: Evaluation of physical surroundings, lighting, and bathroom safety

explanation: The home environment directly impacts safety, making environmental inspection a critical component of the nursing assessment. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h3)

question: A home health nurse inspects staircases and lighting primarily to achieve what goal?

options.A: Determine the market financial value of the patient property
options.B: Prevent avoidable emergency room admissions caused by domestic accidents
options.C: Comply with municipal building and housing safety inspection codes
options.D: Assess the architectural skill used to build the residence

explanation: Identifying and fixing environmental hazards like poor lighting or stairs reduces the risk of falls and subsequent hospital visits. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h3)

question: Sudden ankle swelling in a patient with heart failure indicates what clinical situation?

options.A: A minor allergic reaction to household laundry washing detergent

options.C: A potential worsening of fluid retention and condition exacerbation
options.D: Normal muscle growth from increased daily walking around the house

question: Why is tracking daily weights essential for a homebound heart failure patient?

options.A: It measures the exact caloric intake consumed during recent meals
options.B: It satisfies mandatory monthly nutritional logging requirements for insurance
options.C: It determines whether physical exercise is building muscle mass
options.D: It detects early fluid accumulation before severe respiratory distress occurs

explanation: Weight gain over a day or two usually reflects water weight, warning the nurse and patient of worsening heart failure early. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h4)

question: What term describes the use of multiple medications by a single patient?

options.A: Therapeutic synergy
options.B: Polypharmacy
options.C: Pharmacokinetics
options.D: Biotransformation

explanation: Polypharmacy refers to the concurrent use of multiple drugs, which increases the likelihood of side effects and dosing mistakes. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h5)

question: A patient is confused about taking five different pills at various times. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Advise the patient to stop taking all medications until a doctor arrives
options.B: Tell the patient to take all pills together once daily to save time
options.C: Organize the medications using a labeled weekly pillbox and review the schedule
options.D: Ask a neighbor to administer the drugs whenever they visit

explanation: Pill organizers and clear scheduling simplify complex drug regimens and support patient adherence at home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h5)

question: Where should used injection needles and lancets be disposed of in a home setting?

options.A: In a puncture-resistant container
options.B: Inside standard household plastic trash bags
options.C: Down the domestic toilet or drainage sink
options.D: Into open cardboard boxes with regular paper

explanation: Puncture-resistant containers prevent accidental needle-stick injuries to patients, family members, and waste collectors. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h6)

question: How do home infection control practices differ fundamentally from hospital protocols?

options.A: Homes rely on practical methods like soap, clean water, and bleach rather than industrial units
options.B: Family members must wear sterile surgical gowns during all nursing visits
options.C: Air filtration systems in houses must match hospital operating theater standards
options.D: Infection control rules do not apply once a patient leaves the hospital building

explanation: Home care nurses must adapt sterile hospital concepts into practical, achievable hygiene steps for everyday domestic life. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the teach-back method used for during home visits?

options.A: Evaluating the nurse's ability to speak the local dialect fluently

options.C: Allowing the patient to teach nursing procedures to visiting family members
options.D: Testing whether the patient can read medical textbooks independently

explanation: Having patients explain instructions in their own words ensures comprehension and corrects misunderstandings immediately. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h7)

question: When designing educational materials for a home care patient, what factor should the nurse consider FIRST?

options.A: The learner's literacy level, language, and physical capabilities
options.B: The cost of printing glossy color brochures in large quantities
options.C: The availability of digital tablets and high-speed internet
options.D: The preference of the hospital medical director for medical terminology

explanation: Education is only effective if it is tailored to the specific communication and physical needs of the individual patient. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of interdisciplinary collaboration in home care?

options.A: Reducing the number of house visits required by the primary physician
options.B: Ensuring multiple health professionals coordinate care so no clinical detail is missed
options.C: Lowering the operational tax burden on private healthcare facilities
options.D: Providing social workers with clinical authority to prescribe medications

explanation: Different specialists bring unique insights; sharing information keeps the care plan safe and comprehensive. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h8)

question: What critical component must be included in every home care management plan?

options.A: A signed legal contract binding the family to 24-hour nursing shifts
options.B: A written agreement with local police for priority traffic escort
options.C: A clear emergency protocol detailing steps and contacts for sudden crises
options.D: An inventory of all electrical appliances and their energy consumption

explanation: Sudden emergencies require an immediate, pre-planned response since hospital staff are not physically present in the home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h8)

question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily underactive in individuals experiencing anxiety disorders?

options.A: Gamma-aminobutyric acid
options.B: Histamine
options.C: Acetylcholine
options.D: Dopamine

question: What is the primary role of the amygdala in the development of anxiety symptoms?

options.A: Slowing down the heart rate
options.B: Producing excess serotonin reserves
options.C: Triggering the fight-or-flight response
options.D: Storing long-term factual memories

explanation: The amygdala processes emotional threats and initiates alarm responses even when real physical danger is absent. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is the minimum duration of excessive worry required to diagnose Generalized Anxiety Disorder?

options.A: Six months
options.B: Two weeks
options.C: One year
options.D: Three months

explanation: Diagnostic guidelines specify that chronic and excessive worry must persist for at least six months to confirm Generalized Anxiety Disorder. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h2)

question: A patient experiences sudden episodes of chest pain and terror without an obvious trigger. This suggests...

options.A: Specific phobia
options.B: Generalized anxiety disorder
options.C: Social anxiety disorder
options.D: Panic disorder

explanation: Sudden, unexpected surges of intense fear paired with somatic symptoms point directly toward panic disorder. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which factor represents a biological risk factor for developing anxiety disorders?

options.A: Living in a crowded household
options.B: Experiencing high market inflation
options.C: Family history of mood disorders
options.D: Lack of formal education

explanation: Genetics and biological predisposition play a major role in how vulnerable a person is to anxiety disorders. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h3)

question: Chronic financial instability contributes to anxiety primarily by acting as what type of stressor?

options.A: A localized muscular injury
options.B: A direct neurological infection
options.C: A temporary physical illness
options.D: A continuous environmental stressor

explanation: Persistent economic strain keeps the nervous system in a prolonged state of alert without a clear endpoint. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h3)

question: Which physical symptom is most commonly associated with acute anxiety presentations?

options.A: Tachycardia and palpitations
options.B: Lower limb paralysis
options.C: Yellowing of the sclera
options.D: Persistent joint swelling

explanation: Elevated sympathetic nervous system activity frequently causes a racing heart and palpitations during anxious states. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h4)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic complaining of chest tightness and shortness of breath with normal cardiac labs. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Somatic manifestation of anxiety
options.B: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.C: A primary gastrointestinal ulcer
options.D: An acute myocardial infarction

question: Why are benzodiazepines generally prescribed for short-term use only?

question: What is the primary goal of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy in treating anxiety?

question: What is the main purpose of teaching diaphragmatic breathing to an anxious patient?

question: What is the appropriate communication approach when caring for a patient experiencing an acute panic crisis?

question: Why does vascular dementia typically present with a step-wise decline in cognitive function?

question: A patient who gets lost in familiar places and needs help with finances is showing signs of which stage?

question: A patient with middle-stage dementia accuses family members of stealing personal items. What is the most appropriate understanding of this behavior?

question: What is a primary purpose of installing door alarms in the home of a patient with dementia?

question: What is the most likely meaning behind sudden physical agitation in a non-verbal dementia patient?

question: Why should caregivers break down dressing into simple, single-step instructions for a patient with moderate dementia?

question: What is the primary clinical goal of prescribing cholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil?

question: Why is caregiver burnout especially prevalent in settings like Nigeria where formal elder care services are scarce?

question: What defines a closed fracture?

question: Why is early upper body strengthening especially important for a patient with a lower limb amputation?

question: Why is establishing consistent spatial routines important for patients with severe visual impairment?

question: A patient newly diagnosed with permanent blindness is most likely experiencing which psychological response?

question: How can family members best support a visually impaired relative without hindering recovery?

question: What is the main difference between being deaf and being hard of hearing?

question: Which communication method does a patient with profound hearing loss rely on the most?

options.D: Bone conduction headsets

question: What are the names of the three tiny bones in the middle ear?

options.C: Cochlea, vestibule, and utricle

question: Which part of the inner ear turns fluid vibrations into nerve impulses?

options.A: The cochlea
options.B: The tympanic membrane
options.C: The Eustachian tube
options.D: The external auditory meatus

question: What is the primary cause of conductive hearing loss?

options.A: Impeded sound transmission through the outer or middle ear

options.D: Complete destruction of the vestibulocochlear nerve

question: An elderly patient experiencing presbycusis typically has which type of hearing loss?

question: Which group of medications is well known for causing ototoxicity and hearing damage?

question: Which infection during pregnancy often leads to congenital deafness in the newborn?

question: During a Weber tuning fork test, sound is heard louder in the impaired ear. What does this indicate?

question: What is the main goal of pure-tone audiometry testing?

options.A: Visualizing the physical integrity of the tympanic membrane

options.D: Detecting active bacterial infections in the ear canal

explanation: Pure-tone audiometry measures the softest sounds a patient can hear at different pitches and plots them on a chart. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h5)

question: What is the best way to start a conversation with a hospitalized deaf patient?

question: Which action should nurses avoid when talking to a patient who reads lips?

question: How does a cochlear implant work differently from a regular hearing aid?

question: Which home modification is most helpful for keeping a deaf person safe?

question: What is the main problem inside cells that leads to cancer?

question: How do malignant tumors mainly differ from benign tumors?

options.B: Malignant tumors are always safely enclosed in local tissues
options.C: Benign tumors grow much faster than malignant ones
options.D: Benign tumors frequently spread to distant organs

question: Which type of cancer starts in the tissues that line body surfaces and organs?

options.A: Myelomas

question: A tumor found in a patient's thigh muscle belongs to which cancer category?

options.A: Carcinoma
options.B: Sarcoma
options.C: Lymphoma
options.D: Leukemia

explanation: Muscles, bones, and fat are connective tissues, and cancers that start in these tissues are called sarcomas. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h2)

question: A long-lasting infection with the Human Papillomavirus is a major risk factor for which cancer?

question: Which viral infection is strongly linked to liver cancer cases in Nigeria?

question: What is a common whole-body sign often seen in people with cancer?

question: Which symptom is a typical early warning sign of a local tumor?

question: Which test gives the only sure confirmation that a patient has cancer?

question: How does chemotherapy mainly work in the body?

question: What is the main goal of surgery for early-stage cancer?

question: A family caregiver calls to say their relative on cancer treatment has a new fever. What should the nurse advise?

question: What is the main goal of palliative care in cancer treatment?

question: How does regular exercise help manage high blood pressure over time?

question: Why is it important for community nurses to ask patients about local herbal remedies?

question: Why does hyperglycemia occur in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus?

question: What causes polyuria in an uncontrolled diabetic patient?

question: Why are complex carbohydrates preferred over simple sugars in diabetes nutrition?

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended dietary practice for managing diabetes?

question: What is the primary metabolic benefit of regular physical activity for type 2 diabetes?

question: A patient with neuropathy prepares to start a walking exercise program. What is the priority nursing instruction?

question: Which condition is characterized by severe hyperglycemia, dehydration, and metabolic acidosis?

question: What classifies diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy as microvascular complications?

question: Why is assessing cultural dietary preferences important during diabetes education?

question: What is the primary goal of diabetes self-management education in home care?

options.D: Eliminating the need for periodic clinic visits and laboratory tests

question: What is the primary causative agent of tuberculosis?

options.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.B: Staphylococcus aureus
options.C: Klebsiella pneumoniae
options.D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

explanation: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a slow-growing aerobic bacterium that thrives in oxygen-rich tissues like the lungs. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h1)

question: How are tuberculosis germs primarily spread from one person to another?

options.A: Direct contact with infected skin lesions
options.B: Airborne droplet nuclei from coughing
options.C: Consuming unpasteurized dairy products
options.D: Sharing contaminated eating utensils

explanation: Infectious droplets expelled by coughing or sneezing remain suspended in the air and are inhaled into the alveoli of another person. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h1)

question: Which type of tuberculosis infection makes a person contagious to others?

options.A: Healed primary tuberculosis scar
options.B: Latent tuberculosis infection
options.C: Active tuberculosis disease
options.D: Dormant encapsulated tuberculosis

explanation: Only individuals with active disease who have multiplying bacteria and lung lesions can expel infectious droplets into the air. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h2)

question: What is the primary immunological feature of latent tuberculosis infection?

options.A: Bacteria rapidly destroy the lung parenchyma
options.B: Widespread dissemination occurs through the blood
options.C: The immune system completely destroys the pathogen
options.D: Bacilli are contained within walled-off granulomas

question: A persistent cough lasting longer than how many weeks warrants investigation for tuberculosis?

options.A: Six weeks
options.B: One week
options.C: Three months
options.D: Two weeks

question: A patient complains of drenching night sweats, afternoon fevers, and losing weight over two months. What is the most likely diagnosis to investigate?

options.A: Simple tension headache
options.B: Pulmonary tuberculosis
options.C: Acute bacterial pharyngitis
options.D: Uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis

explanation: Constitutional signs like night sweats, low-grade fevers, and unexplained weight loss are classic indicators of systemic tuberculosis infection. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h3)

question: What does a positive acid-fast bacilli smear test indicate in a patient with a chronic cough?

options.A: Viral influenza infection
options.B: Acute streptococcal pharyngitis
options.C: Fungal pneumonia infection
options.D: Presumed mycobacterial infection

explanation: Acid-fast staining highlights mycobacteria, which retain the stain despite acid washing due to mycolic acid in their cell walls. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h4)

question: Why is the GeneXpert assay preferred over traditional microscopy in modern tuberculosis control programs?

options.A: It requires no electricity or specialized laboratory equipment
options.B: It detects both tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance rapidly
options.C: It can completely differentiate latent from active disease states
options.D: It replaces the need for a physical chest examination

question: What is the primary purpose of Directly Observed Therapy in tuberculosis management?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing drugs
options.B: To eliminate the need for routine liver function tests
options.C: To ensure the patient swallows every prescribed dose
options.D: To prevent the transmission of latent infection variants

explanation: Directly Observed Therapy guarantees adherence, preventing premature cessation of drugs and subsequent development of drug resistance. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h5)

question: Why are multiple anti-tuberculosis drugs prescribed simultaneously rather than just a single medication?

options.A: To completely eliminate all normal flora in the lungs
options.B: To reduce the physical size of each individual pill
options.C: To shorten the overall treatment duration to one week
options.D: To prevent the emergence of drug-resistant bacterial strains

explanation: Using multiple drugs targets different bacterial populations and drastically lowers the risk that mutant strains will survive. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h5)

question: How does maximizing natural ventilation in a home help control tuberculosis transmission?

options.A: It dilutes and disperses airborne infectious droplet nuclei
options.B: It humidifies the air to stop bacilli from leaving the mouth
options.C: It increases the room temperature to kill bacterial spores
options.D: It prevents the patient from coughing during sleeping hours

explanation: Fresh air circulation reduces the concentration of suspended droplet nuclei, lowering the chance of inhalation by family members. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h6)

question: A newly diagnosed patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis prepares to return home. What advice should the nurse give regarding sleeping arrangements?

options.A: Share a family bed to maintain emotional closeness
options.B: Wear a surgical mask continuously while sleeping
options.C: Sleep alone in a well-ventilated room
options.D: Sleep in a closed room with an electric fan running

question: Why is nutritional support a critical component of nursing care for tuberculosis patients?

options.A: Proteins directly kill the mycobacterial cell wall structures
options.B: Good nutrition prevents drug-induced liver function failure
options.C: The disease causes severe wasting and increases metabolic demands
options.D: Dietary supplements replace the need for anti-tuberculosis drugs

explanation: Tuberculosis depletes body energy stores, requiring increased protein and caloric intake to rebuild damaged lung tissue and restore strength. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h7)

question: A patient states they want to stop taking their drugs after four weeks because their cough has stopped. How should the nurse respond?

question: Which harmless side effect should the nurse warn patients to expect when taking rifampicin?

question: A patient taking isoniazid reports a tingling sensation and numbness in both feet. What deficiency is this indicative of?

options.C: Pyridoxine deficiency
options.D: Ascorbic acid deficiency

question: What is a primary characteristic of clinical depression compared to normal sadness?

options.A: Persistent feelings lasting for at least two weeks

options.D: Sudden bursts of energy followed by extreme exhaustion

explanation: Clinical depression involves long-lasting mood disturbances that disrupt daily functioning, unlike fleeting moments of sadness. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is depression frequently missed in home healthcare patients?

options.A: Patients always report their emotional struggles directly to family members
options.B: Symptoms are often masked by chronic physical illnesses and isolation
options.C: Laboratory tests can easily detect low serotonin levels in home settings
options.D: Home nurses only focus on surgical wound care and vital signs

explanation: Physical complaints and social isolation in the home often overshadow subtle emotional changes. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which neurotransmitters are primarily linked to the biochemical theory of depression?

options.A: Acetylcholine and gamma-aminobutyric acid only
options.B: Insulin, glucagon, and cortisol
options.C: Serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine
options.D: Thyroxine and adrenaline

explanation: These specific brain chemicals regulate mood, pleasure, and energy levels, which are disrupted in depression. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h2)

question: A home care patient with hypertension and arthritis starts showing signs of severe low mood after starting a new prescription drug. What is the likely contributing factor?

options.A: An sudden increase in dietary sodium intake

options.C: Polypharmacy or medication-induced depressive side effects
options.D: An acute infection of the central nervous system

question: What defines persistent depressive disorder compared to major depressive disorder?

options.A: Temporary sadness that resolves within a few days

options.C: Sudden panic attacks occurring only during the night hours
options.D: A milder mood disturbance lasting for two years or longer

question: Why is situational depression common among newly homebound patients?

options.A: The home environment always contains toxic chemical agents
options.B: Patients suddenly stop producing red blood cells at home
options.C: Major life changes and loss of independence act as acute triggers

question: Which screening tool is specifically designed and validated for assessing older adults in home care?

question: What is the primary purpose of using the PHQ-9 tool during a home visit?

options.A: To evaluate the nutritional value of the patient's local diet

question: What is the best approach when a depressed patient struggles to complete daily hygiene tasks?

options.A: Break the tasks down into smaller, manageable steps

question: A family caregiver tells a depressed patient, 'You have nothing to be sad about.' How should the nurse guide this caregiver?

options.B: Explain that validation of feelings is more helpful than dismissing them
options.C: Suggest that the caregiver stop talking to the patient entirely

question: Why are SSRIs generally preferred over TCAs for elderly home care patients?

question: What crucial educational point must the nurse share with a patient starting a new antidepressant?

question: What is the correct nursing action when assessing a depressed patient for suicidal ideation?

question: A home care patient admits to having a specific plan to end their life today. What should the nurse do FIRST?

question: What is the primary characteristic of a psychotic state?

question: Why is managing psychosis in a home setting uniquely challenging for community nurses?

question: Hearing voices when no one is speaking around the patient is called what?

question: Why should a nurse avoid arguing against a patient's firmly held persecutory delusion?

question: Which neurotransmitter is most heavily implicated in the development of positive psychotic symptoms?

question: A young adult client presents with sudden acute psychosis after heavy use of psychoactive substances. What should the nurse suspect as a primary trigger?

options.B: Substance-induced psychotic disorder from drug exposure

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a Mental Status Examination during a home visit?

question: Why is environmental safety assessment particularly crucial when visiting a home psychiatric client?

question: Which medication class is most commonly associated with extrapyramidal side effects like muscle stiffness?

question: What is the primary benefit of long-acting injectable antipsychotics for community-dwelling clients?

question: Which action is recommended when verbally de-escalating an agitated client at home?

question: What should a community nurse do immediately if verbal de-escalation fails and physical violence is imminent?

options.A: Withdraw immediately from the home and call for emergency assistance

question: What is a common consequence experienced by family members caring for a relative with chronic psychosis?

question: Why is teaching families to spot early warning signs of relapse so important?

question: What does a comprehensive recovery approach for a client with psychosis primarily focus on?

question: When is the best time for a nurse to collaborate with a client to create a written relapse prevention plan?

question: What primary body system is affected by cerebral palsy?

question: Why is cerebral palsy classified as a non-progressive disorder?

question: A common perinatal cause of cerebral palsy is...

question: Which factor represents a postnatal risk for developing cerebral palsy?

question: The most common clinical type of cerebral palsy is...

question: Damage to the cerebellum in cerebral palsy typically leads to which clinical feature?

options.C: Poor balance and uncoordinated movements

question: What is a common clinical finding during physical examination of an infant with spastic cerebral palsy?

question: Which diagnostic imaging tool is most useful for identifying structural brain lesions in cerebral palsy?

question: A nurse assessing a child with suspected cerebral palsy should prioritize evaluating which parameter?

question: The main goal of physiotherapy in managing cerebral palsy is to...

question: Why is an interprofessional team necessary for the care of a child with cerebral palsy?

options.C: Physicians cannot prescribe medications without therapist approval

question: A key psychosocial nursing intervention for parents of a child with cerebral palsy is...

question: What is the primary focus of nurse-led education regarding home positioning?

question: Which physical complication is commonly associated with long-term spastic cerebral palsy?

question: What factor most heavily influences the long-term prognosis for independent living in cerebral palsy?

question: What core area of development is primarily affected in Autism Spectrum Disorder?

options.D: Report the household conditions immediately to local child welfare authorities

question: What is the primary goal of nursing assessment regarding dysphagia in hospital settings?

options.A: To speed up the recovery process for surgical wound healing
options.B: To ensure patients eat all the food provided on their tray
options.C: To eliminate the need for any assistance during meal times
options.D: To prevent aspiration and choking by matching diet to swallowing ability

explanation: Identifying swallowing deficits early allows nurses to implement proper diet textures and prevent airway obstruction. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T7#GNS324_U6_T7_h6)

question: What primary feature makes home healthcare fire safety harder than hospital safety?

options.A: Absence of institutional staff and built-in sprinkler systems
options.B: Patients always refuse to install smoke detectors
options.C: Electricity supply in homes is unstable and dangerous
options.D: Fire trucks take longer to reach residential areas

explanation: Hospitals have heavy infrastructure and large teams ready for evacuation, whereas homes rely on limited individual resources during an emergency. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h1)

question: Why does home oxygen therapy drastically increase fire danger for a client?

options.A: It heats up the room air to dangerous boiling temperatures
options.B: It releases toxic fumes that cause sudden fainting
options.C: It increases the electrical voltage flowing through wall sockets
options.D: It creates an enriched environment where materials ignite easily

explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, meaning sparks from electrical devices or smoking can cause fires to spread with explosive speed. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h1)

question: What is the leading origin of residential fires in home environments?

options.A: Cooking appliances left unattended
options.B: Leaking cooking gas cylinders
options.C: Children playing with matches
options.D: Faulty ceiling fan regulators

explanation: Unattended cooking and hot grease are statistically responsible for the highest number of home-based fire outbreaks. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h2)

question: A patient uses candles for lighting near a mosquito net. What makes this combination dangerous?

options.A: Fabrics like mosquito nets ignite rapidly from open flames
options.B: Mosquito nets produce toxic smoke when exposed to room air
options.C: Candle wax reacts chemically with synthetic net materials
options.D: Candles lower the oxygen concentration needed for breathing

explanation: Lightweight synthetic fabrics catch fire almost instantly when exposed to an open flame, engulfing sleeping areas within seconds. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h2)

question: How should a nurse advise a family storing a cooking gas cylinder indoors?

options.A: Place it directly beside the stove for easy hose connection
options.B: Keep it upright in a well-ventilated space away from heat
options.C: Store it inside a wooden kitchen cabinet to hide it
options.D: Lay it horizontally on the floor to prevent rolling over

explanation: Proper ventilation prevents gas accumulation in case of minor leaks, while keeping cylinders away from direct heat prevents pressure buildup. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h3)

question: Which safe cooking practice should nurses teach home care clients?

options.A: Leaving hot oil pans unattended for short breaks
options.B: Storing flour containers directly above the stove
options.C: Using plastic plates close to open gas burners
options.D: Turning pot handles inward toward the stove

explanation: Turning handles inward prevents accidental bumps from passersby that could spill boiling liquids or hot oil. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h3)

question: What does the letter 'A' stand for in the PASS fire extinguisher technique?

options.A: Activate the fire sprinkler system
options.B: Assess the electrical wiring first
options.C: Alarm the neighborhood for help
options.D: Aim low at the base of the fire

explanation: Aiming at the flames is ineffective; the extinguishing agent must target the base of the fire where the fuel source sits. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h4)

question: How often should household smoke detector batteries be replaced to ensure reliability?

options.A: Only when the alarm sounds
options.B: Every year
options.C: Every month
options.D: Every five years

explanation: Annual battery replacement guarantees that the unit remains powered and functional even if the low-battery chirp fails. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h4)

question: Why is crawling low under smoke emphasized during fire escape drills?

options.A: It prevents panic attacks during total darkness
options.B: Hot, toxic smoke and gases rise toward the ceiling
options.C: It protects the legs from falling ceiling debris
options.D: Floors are less slippery than upper wall areas

explanation: Cleanest air and lower temperatures remain closer to the floor, reducing smoke inhalation injury during exit. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h5)

question: What must every household establish regarding a safe evacuation location?

options.A: The topmost floor balcony for easy rescue access
options.B: A designated outdoor meeting place away from the building
options.C: The closed kitchen space with water supply
options.D: A nearby commercial petrol station for shelter

explanation: An agreed outdoor spot allows family members and responders to quickly confirm everyone escaped safely. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h5)

question: A patient's clothing catches fire suddenly. What action should the nurse initiate first?

options.A: Wrap the patient tightly in a plastic bedsheet
options.B: Pull out the wall electrical socket immediately
options.C: Run outside to fetch a bucket of cold water
options.D: Instruct the patient to stop, drop, and roll

explanation: Stopping, dropping, and rolling smothers the flames and prevents facial burns from inhaling fire upwards. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h6)

question: What is the correct priority order for a nurse when discovering an active fire?

options.A: Gather all medical equipment, open windows, run outside
options.B: Sound the alarm, salvage medical records, lock doors
options.C: Rescue endangered persons, sound the alarm, confine, evacuate
options.D: Extinguish the fire, call the family head, rescue the patient

explanation: Life safety always takes precedence; human rescue comes first before alarming others and confining the blaze. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T8#GNS324_U6_T8_h6)

question: What primary challenge do home healthcare environments present for infection control compared to hospitals?

options.A: Excessive availability of sterile supplies
options.B: Lack of controlled engineering systems
options.C: Constant presence of hospital epidemiologists
options.D: Mandatory industrial waste compactors

explanation: Private residences lack hospital-grade ventilation and specialized utility infrastructure, complicating standard infection control measures. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h1)

question: Why must nurses adapt infection control principles when working in private homes?

options.A: Standard aseptic techniques are unnecessary in residential care
options.B: Hospital policies are legally invalid outside facility walls
options.C: Domestic spaces require practical adjustments without reducing safety
options.D: Patients in homes are completely immune to nosocomial pathogens

explanation: Adapting protocols ensures safety while working within the practical limits of a patient's living environment. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h1)

question: Which link in the chain of infection is represented by contaminated medical equipment?

options.A: Reservoir
options.B: Susceptible host
options.C: Portal of exit
options.D: Infectious agent

explanation: Objects and surfaces that harbor pathogens act as reservoirs where microbes can live and multiply. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h2)

question: How does hand hygiene directly impact the chain of infection?

options.A: It destroys the susceptible host's immunity
options.B: It closes the portal of exit on the patient
options.C: It interrupts the mode of transmission
options.D: It eliminates the infectious agent entirely

explanation: Washing hands removes pathogens from the nurse's hands, preventing them from moving between patients or surfaces. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h2)

question: When should standard precautions be applied in clinical practice?

options.A: Only when an infection is laboratory confirmed
options.B: When patients display obvious symptoms of illness
options.C: For all patients regardless of diagnosis
options.D: Exclusively in critical care hospital units

explanation: Standard precautions apply to every patient interaction because infection status is not always known upfront. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of wearing non-sterile gloves during patient care?

options.A: To completely eliminate the need for subsequent handwashing
options.B: To prevent allergic reactions to latex in patients
options.C: To protect the nurse from contact with infectious material
options.D: To ensure absolute sterility of the clinical environment

explanation: Gloves act as a barrier against blood and body fluids, though hand hygiene is still required after removal. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h3)

question: Which personal protective equipment is required for care under droplet precautions?

options.A: Sterile booties
options.B: N95 respirator
options.C: Surgical mask
options.D: Rubber apron

explanation: Droplet precautions guard against large respiratory particles, making a standard surgical mask appropriate for close interactions. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h4)

question: Why are airborne precautions difficult to execute properly in standard residential homes?

options.A: Homes lack negative pressure rooms and specialized air filtration
options.B: Families refuse to let healthcare workers wear protective gear
options.C: Standard medical masks completely block all aerosolized nuclei
options.D: Airborne pathogens do not exist outside of hospital laboratories

explanation: Airborne isolation requires negative airflow rooms to contain microscopic particles, which standard housing configurations cannot provide. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h4)

question: What is the correct action to take immediately after using a disposable injection needle?

options.A: Drop it directly into a puncture-resistant sharps container
options.B: Leave it on the bedside tray until the end of the shift
options.C: Recap the needle securely using both of your hands
options.D: Place it inside a regular plastic household rubbish bag

explanation: Sharps must be discarded immediately into a rigid, dedicated container to prevent accidental punctures. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h5)

question: Why is the two-handed needle recapping technique strongly discouraged in clinical practice?

options.A: It wastes valuable time during fast-paced clinical procedures
options.B: It significantly raises the risk of accidental needlestick injuries
options.C: It violates the manufacturer's sterility warranty on the syringe
options.D: It dulls the sharp tip of the needle making injection painful

explanation: Holding the cap with one hand while trying to guide the needle with the other often leads to fingers being punctured. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h5)

question: What process must always occur BEFORE applying a chemical disinfectant to a surface?

options.A: Thermal sterilization in an autoclave chamber
options.B: Physical cleaning with detergent and water
options.C: Ultraviolet radiation exposure for one hour
options.D: Sealing the surface in an airtight container

explanation: Organic debris can shield microorganisms from disinfectants, so physical cleaning must happen first. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h6)

question: Why is true sterilization rarely performed directly inside a patient's private home?

options.A: Microorganisms in homes do not form resilient spores
options.B: Homes lack the specialized equipment required to achieve and verify sterility
options.C: Chemical disinfectants are completely ineffective against bacterial spores
options.D: Patient families are legally barred from operating autoclaves

explanation: Sterilization demands validated high-temperature or gas chambers that are impractical and unavailable in residential settings. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h6)

question: Why is a return demonstration by the family caregiver considered vital during infection control education?

options.A: It proves the caregiver has memorized all clinical terminology
options.B: It confirms the caregiver can perform the technique safely on their own
options.C: It fulfills mandatory legal documentation required for insurance billing
options.D: It replaces the need for verbal instructions and written handouts

explanation: Watching the caregiver perform the skill ensures they understand the physical steps before doing them independently. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h7)

question: Which symptom is a classic indicator of a localized wound infection that caregivers should monitor?

options.A: General decrease in systemic blood pressure
options.B: Purulent drainage from the incision site
options.C: Sudden loss of hearing acuity in both ears
options.D: Inability to taste sweet or salty foods

explanation: Pus or purulent discharge is a direct physical sign of localized bacterial activity and inflammation. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h7)

question: What is the immediate first-aid action following an accidental needlestick injury?

options.A: Squeeze the wound vigorously to force out contaminated blood
options.B: Apply a concentrated bleach solution directly onto the wound
options.C: Cover the puncture tightly with an adhesive bandage immediately
options.D: Wash the exposed site thoroughly with soap and water

explanation: Immediate washing reduces the viral or bacterial load at the site of exposure before reporting the incident. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h8)

question: Why is vigorous squeezing or scrubbing of a fresh needlestick injury discouraged?

options.A: It can force pathogens deeper into the underlying tissues
options.B: It causes excessive bleeding that is difficult to stop
options.C: It neutralizes the effectiveness of antiseptic soaps
options.D: It alters the blood test results required later by the laboratory

explanation: Trauma from squeezing increases tissue damage and can drive infectious agents further into the microvasculature. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T9#GNS324_U6_T9_h8)
